items.title: Day 11: Connections, Transactions and Query Conditions in the Data Access Layer
items.summary: How FormSchema Drives SQL drew the boundary of the definition-driven route: relationships across tables are always single column equality, and what they join to is always a physical table. Reports, statistics and batch imports go beyond that range, where SQL gets written by hand, and every framework has to leave that route open. The trouble is at the junction. "I do not do this part" and "you do this part entirely yourself" are two different things, and opening an entry point that takes an arbitrary SQL string writes them as one. The cost does not show up there and then. It shows up at the second database, at the first hand assembled WHERE, at the first query inserted halfway through a save. What the framework puts at that junction is DbAccess, the one entry point for an application issuing its own statements: one SQL statement, a few values to pass, no connection object, nothing to remember to close, not one piece of string concatenation. items.title: Build a Stripe cancel flow: cancel_at_period_end and a webhook handler that doesn't double-count
items.summary: A cancel flow on Stripe is three pieces: a place that catches the cancel click, an offer step, and a webhook that tells your app whether the cancellation was scheduled, stopped or finished. Set cancel_at_period_end to true so the subscriber keeps what they paid for, and revoke access only when customer.subscription.deleted arrives. By default, cancelling a subscription through the API takes effect immediately and no more invoices are generated. To let the subscriber keep the period they already paid for, update the subscription with cancel_at_period_end=true. Schedule it: set cancel_at_period_end to true. Stripe sends customer.subscription.updated. Offer something (optional): the subscriber is still active, so there is time to show an offer and apply it. Stop it: set cancel_at_period_end to false any time before the period ends. Stripe sends customer.subscription.updated again. You cannot reactivate a subscription that has already been cancelled. Let it end: when the period ends Stripe cancels the subscription and sends customer.subscription.deleted. That is the event that tells you to revoke access. items.title: I default to Next.js for a reason that has almost nothing to do with performance
items.summary: Framework choice is usually developer preference dressed up as strategy, and I say that as someone whose default has been Next.js for years. The reasons I would give another developer are not the reasons that matter to the person paying for the project, and the gap between those two lists is worth writing down, because the second list is the one that survives contact with a budget. A plain React application renders in the browser. The visitor downloads a JavaScript bundle, the bundle runs, and only then does content appear. Behind a login that is completely fine and often the right architecture. For anything that needs to be found, it is bad, because the first thing a crawler or a three-year-old phone receives is an empty document with a script tag in it. The standard answer is to bolt server rendering onto React by hand. That is not a weekend. It is a genuine engineering project with its own maintenance bill, its own subtle hydration bugs and its own bus factor, and it competes for time with the actual product. items.summary: Most TOTP bugs are key-length, clock, and replay bugs, not crypto bugs. The algorithm is short enough to work through on paper, and doing it once makes the failure modes easier to see. Here is the full path from a shared secret and Unix time 59 to 94287082, using the RFC's test key, then the parts the RFC leaves to your server. RFC 6238 defines the time step as T = floor((Unix time - T0) / X). T0 defaults to 0, X to 30 seconds. At Unix time 59: T = floor((59 - 0) / 30) = 1. That counter goes into HMAC as an 8-byte big-endian integer: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01. Keep the width at 8 bytes even when T is small: RFC 6238 §4.2 requires support for T beyond 32 bits past 2038, and a variable-width counter breaks there. TOTP is HOTP (RFC 4226) with a different counter source. HOTP computes HMAC-SHA-1(key, counter) and truncates. TOTP takes the counter from the clock instead of incrementing it per code. The same key and counter always produce the same digits, so two machines agree without exchanging anything. The RFC 6238 test key is the ASCII string 12345678901234567890, 20 bytes. items.title: Node.js Password Reset Email Delivery and Spam Audit Architecture
items.summary: A password reset email is most likely to land in spam when authentication is missing or invalid, the message resembles a phishing lure, the body contains suspicious or excessive links, or the receiving server distrusts the sender's bulk behavior. For a logistics system that must prove a compliance notice was delivered, choose the architecture that makes those causes observable without making the reset path depend on a single opaque provider. Short answer: keep the reset decision and audit record in your Node.js service, then choose between a direct email provider and a unified REST gateway at the delivery boundary. The invariant is the same in both designs: verified sender authentication, a restrained template with one intentional reset URL, a durable notice ID, and a delivery history that distinguishes accepted, delivered, bounced, and unknown. This is a system-shape decision. The provider can report what it accepted; it cannot prove that a recipient read the message or that a mail client will place it in the inbox. items.summary: Any calculator that scores a timed event has the same quiet problem: people type times in five different ways. One person types 14:30. Another types 870. A third types 14.30 and means fourteen minutes and thirty seconds. If your parser guesses wrong, the score is wrong, and the user usually cannot tell. This post walks through a small, boring approach that has held up well for me when building fitness-test calculators: accept a few clearly defined formats, reject everything else with a helpful message, and compare times as whole seconds. Before writing code, list the formats you will accept. Mine are: mm:ss such as 14:30 or 9:05 m:ss with a single-digit minute h:mm:ss for very long events, such as 1:02:15 plain seconds such as 870, only when the field is labelled as seconds Everything else is an error. That includes 14.30, 14,30, and 14m30s. It is tempting to be generous, but a decimal point in a time field is genuinely ambiguous, because it can mean 14.3 minutes or 14 minutes 30 seconds. items.title: My auto-hide controls kept flickering in ArtPlayer v5: the dual-timer fight and the 1.5s immunity fix
items.summary: I'm building RKMovies (a tiny 4K player for old phones) — 0.91 MB APK, hardware decode, no accounts, no tracking. The player UI runs on ArtPlayer v5, and I replaced its default controls with my own auto-hide layer. That layer flickered for weeks. Here's why. ArtPlayer hides its controls on its own timer. Every timeupdate it checks controls.timer; if the controls have been idle for a few seconds it hides them and hides the cursor. I wanted different rules: never hide while the settings panel is open, while paused, or while the user is scrubbing, plus a minimum visible time of 1s. So I added my own hideTimer (3.5s) with those guards. Two timers, two sources of truth. ArtPlayer's internal check and my setTimeout disagreed about when to hide, so the controls flickered: my layer showed them, the library's next timeupdate hid them, mine showed them again. The fix wasn't a second timer fighting the first. It was a 1.5s immunity lock. items.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
items.summary: Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics. 1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with. 2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. items.title: Firefox's New Mini Window Is Every Multitasker's Dream
items.summary: Mozilla is testing a new Firefox Nightly feature called Mini Window that lets users pop an entire webpage into a small, always-on-top window stripped of most browser controls. "The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window," writes ZDNet's Jack Wallen. "Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app." From the report: At first blush, there's no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it. However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/forward/reload buttons, and the window close button -- and that's it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content. On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. items.title: AI-written styles typecheck. Some still render nothing
items.summary: Box Kite's MCP server runs your AI assistant's props through the real styling engine mid-task, and names each value that would render nothing. Below: the mistakes it catches, a worked session with every answer pasted from the server, and what it can't know about your project. It documents @box-kite/mcp 2.2.12. The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article. Three props an assistant wrote for a settings row, handed to the server: check_styles { "props": { "jc": "between", "fontSize": 4, "lineHeight": 1.5 } } Some of these write no CSS, or CSS they almost certainly did not mean. - ❌ `jc` does not accept "between" — no rule and no class name were written. It takes start, end, flex-start, flex-end, center, left, right, space-between, space-around, space-evenly, stretch, safe center, … (17 in all — call `get_props`). - ⚠️ `fontSize` → `.fontSize-4{font-size:0.25rem}` — fontSize={4} is 4px text: fontSize's divider is 16, not the spacing scale's 4, so the number is the pixel size. items.title: Autorização ABAC no ASP.NET Core: indo além das roles
items.summary: Quando se fala em autorização em APIs, a primeira solução que vem à cabeça geralmente é usar roles: o usuário é "admin", então pode tudo; é "user", então pode menos. Isso funciona bem até a regra de negócio ficar mais específica, como "o usuário pode ler este documento se ele for o autor ou se for do mesmo departamento", ou "o admin só pode acessar a área administrativa em horário comercial". Nesses cenários, roles não são suficientes, e é aí que entra o ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control). Neste artigo vamos construir uma API em ASP.NET Core que aplica regras ABAC sobre documentos, usando somente os recursos nativos de autorização do framework. Pré-requisitos: .NET 10 SDK instalado. Docker instalado (o banco é um SQL Server em container). Ferramenta do EF Core: dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef. Conhecimento básico de C# e de APIs REST. items.title: Why freezing completed Markdown blocks reduces streaming rendering work
items.summary: An AI response arrives as text deltas. A Markdown renderer normally receives a document. Connecting them with render(allTextSoFar) repeatedly asks the renderer to interpret text the reader has already seen. I built react-stream-markdown to explore a different boundary: keep completed blocks on screen and re-parse the unfinished suffix. The repository is currently version 0.4.1 and MIT licensed. Here is how it works, where its cost still grows, and what the published benchmark actually measures. Suppose a response contains N characters and arrives in chunks of c characters. A full-document parser sees c characters, then 2c, then 3c, and so on. With a linear parser, the sum of characters examined is approximately N²/(2c). This models repeated parsing work; it does not mean every part of browser rendering is quadratic. React can reuse DOM elements after reconciliation. That does not automatically prevent an upstream Markdown parser from scanning the accumulated string. Parsing, building a tree, reconciling, layout, and painting have separate costs. items.title: React Context Explained: How It Works Under the Hood
items.summary: React’s Context API lets you share data between components without passing props manually through every level. It’s designed for global values like theme, language, or authentication — where many components need access to the same data. Context provides a way to share values like theme, user, or locale deeply in the component tree without prop drilling. It helps solve this problem: // Before: prop drilling With Context: const ThemeContext = React.createContext("light"); Creates a Context object with two parts: A Provider component. A reference for the current value inside React’s internal Fiber tree. React stores the value on the Provider’s Fiber node. Keeps track of all child consumers that read from this context. const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); React looks upward in the component tree to find the nearest Provider. Returns its value. If the Provider’s value changes, React re-renders all consumers that depend on it. Every Context keeps a _currentValue reference on its Provider. useContext subscribes the component to that Provider. items.title: React Fiber Explained: How React’s Engine Actually Works
items.summary: React Fiber is the internal engine that powers React’s rendering and reconciliation. It’s what makes React’s updates smooth, interruptible, and concurrent. React Fiber is React’s reconciliation engine — the system that decides what needs to be rendered and when. Before React 16, React updates were synchronous and blocking. Once rendering started, React couldn’t pause or reprioritize work — large trees could freeze the UI. Fiber was a complete rewrite that made React’s rendering: ⏸ Interruptible ⏱ Prioritized 🔁 Incremental (chunked) 💾 Recoverable (resumable) In short: Fiber = React’s virtual call stack for async rendering. Before Fiber, React used a recursive rendering approach — like this: function renderTree(node) { node.render(); node.children.forEach(renderTree); } Large trees blocked the main thread. The browser couldn’t respond to user input until React finished. No way to pause, abort, or prioritize rendering. React Fiber breaks the rendering work into small units of work, called fiber nodes. This lets React: Pause between chunks of work. Resume later if the browser is busy. Assign different priorities to updates. Reuse previous work if nothing changed. So React no longer b

items.title: React memo vs useMemo vs useCallback — When to Use Which
items.summary: React memo vs useMemo vs useCallback All three are about skipping unnecessary work. But they work differently. React re-renders a component whenever its parent re-renders — even if nothing changed. Memoization lets you say: "Only redo this if the inputs actually changed." React.memo — Skip re-rendering a component Wraps a component. Skips re-render if props didn't change. const Button = React.memo(({ onClick, label }: { onClick: () => void; label: string }) => { console.log("Button rendered"); return {label} ; }); Without memo: Button re-renders every time the parent does. With memo: Button skips re-render if onClick and label are the same. useMemo — Cache a computed value Memoizes the result of an expensive calculation. const total = useMemo(() => { return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0); }, [items]); Runs only when items changes. Returns the cached value on other renders. ❌ Without useMemo: recalculates on every render. ✅ With useMemo: recalculates only when items changes. useCallback — Cache a function Memoizes a function reference so it stays stable across renders. const handleClick = useCallback(() => { console.log("clicked", id); }, [id]); Without useCallback

items.title: React useEffect Dependencies — The Bug That Keeps Coming Back
items.summary: useEffect looks simple. Add a function, add a dependency array, done. Then production hits you with: a timer that logs the wrong count a fetch that sends a stale token an effect that runs forever or React Strict Mode making everything run twice These are not random React bugs. They all come from one idea: Every render is a snapshot. Your effect remembers the values from the render that scheduled it. Once you internalize that sentence, most useEffect pain disappears. When React renders your component, it creates a snapshot of props and state for that moment. function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => { console.log(count); // 👈 frozen at the count from THIS render }, 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []); // empty deps = only first render's count return setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count} ; } You click the button → UI shows 1, 2, 3… But the interval still logs 0 forever. Why? The callback inside setInterval is a closure. It captured count = 0 from the first render and never saw updates. This is the famous stale closure problem — the #1 useEffect interview trap. items.title: The Server Action That Ran Twice, but Only on localhost
items.summary: Picture a "mark as read" feature. Open a notification, and a Server Action flips it to read in the database and bumps a counter. You add a console.log to the action to watch it work, open the page in next dev, and the terminal prints: [markAsRead] call #1 [markAsRead] call #2 One page load, two calls. Every time. I rebuilt that exact setup on this blog's codebase (Next.js 16.4, React 19) as a ten-line test page, and got the same thing: two POST requests with the same next-action id in the network tab, two log lines on the server. Two calls from one load looks like a framework bug. Maybe Next.js retries actions. Maybe the page renders twice on the server and each render fires the action. Maybe HMR left an old copy of the component mounted. None of those hold up. Here's the whole client component: "use client"; import { useEffect } from "react"; import { markAsRead } from "./actions"; export function Notification({ id }: { id: string }) { useEffect(() => { markAsRead(id); }, [id]); return … ; } Server Actions never run during rendering. They run when the browser calls them, and the only thing calling this one is useEffect. So the real question is: why does the effect run twice? Next.

items.title: Google Will Turn Off Search For Schools That Reject AI
items.summary: Google will disable AI tools by default for K-12 students early next year unless school administrators explicitly enable them, but schools that choose to block AI entirely will also lose student access to Google Search. The New York Times reports: Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A.I. But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search. A.I. features are now a standard part of Google's commercially available search engine. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available." items.title: Obfuscating a .NET Worker Service: protecting a headless background worker
items.summary: A Worker Service is the quiet case in the obfuscation conversation. It has no controllers, no views, no public API that callers depend on — it is a BackgroundService on a timer, or an IHostedService draining a queue, built on the Generic Host and installed as a Windows Service or a systemd unit. Because it has no surface, two things are true at once: it is the easiest kind of .NET app to obfuscate aggressively, because almost nothing in it is observed by name, and it is the easiest to forget, because "it's just a background job on our customer's server" feels like it isn't exposed. It is exposed. This post is about treating a headless worker as what it is — a DLL in someone else's hands — and protecting it with the grain of the Generic Host rather than against it. The thing that makes a worker a tempting target is exactly what makes it feel safe: it has no front end. In a desktop or web app, a lot of the code is presentation, plumbing and framework glue, and the valuable logic is a fraction of it. A worker is almost all valuable logic. items.title: Per-app trackpad scenes: the missing layer in Mac input
items.summary: Your Mac trackpad is the best input device on the machine, and macOS still treats it as a rectangle for moving a pointer. The gestures are global. Three fingers up. Two fingers swipe. Pinch. They work everywhere, which is exactly why they cannot be specific to anything. The same swipe that means "go back" in a browser means nothing in Figma, and the edge that would make a good volume slider is ignored by the system. A per-app scene is a different model. Instead of starting with a gesture, you start with the app in front of you and arrange the surface: edges, corners, custom areas, a center gesture. The layout changes when the app changes. A default scene covers everything else. I have been building TrackStudio around this model. This post is about the model, not the product. A global layout assumes every app wants the same controls. They do not. A browser wants navigation. An editor wants windows and screenshots. A terminal wants restraint. A video editor wants transport and a way back to Mission Control. Common App Store Connect messages developers search for include ITMS-91053 and ITMS-91056. items.title: Your AI Agent Can Write SwiftUI That Compiles on Mac, iPhone, and iPad — and Still Get All Three Wrong
items.summary: Ask an AI coding agent to build a settings screen in SwiftUI, and it'll hand you something that compiles everywhere Apple ships a screen — iPhone, iPad, Mac, even Vision Pro. That's not the hard part anymore. Getting an LLM to produce SwiftUI that builds across Apple platforms is almost table stakes in 2026. Getting it to look like it belongs on each of those platforms is a completely different problem, and it's one that doesn't show up as a red squiggle anywhere. Run that agent-written settings screen on iPad and you get a phone layout stretched into a wider window. Run it on Mac and there's no sidebar, no menu-bar affordances, nothing that reads as "a Mac app" instead of "an iPhone app someone recompiled." The code is correct. It compiles, it runs, nothing crashes. It's just wrong in a way that only shows up if a human actually opens it on the other two devices — which an agent, working from a single mental model of "the app," has no particular reason to do unless you force it to. This is the part of "AI writes your UI now" that gets glossed over. items.title: What broke when my SwiftUI app met the iPhone Duo (and what Apple's checklist missed)
items.summary: I have been building a unit converter for iOS since 2016 (convertunits.app). Late 2025 I rewrote it in SwiftUI. Then Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and I had about six weeks to make the app look right on a device I could only run in the Xcode 27.1 simulator. Two weeks after launch, 824 of my existing users had restored the app on a Duo. This post covers what broke, the code that fixed it, and how I counted those users, since App Store Connect does not list the Duo as a device. Folded, the outer display is a little wider than an iPhone (466 × 678 pt) and compact width. The status bar is not at the top: it sits in a column on the right edge, so the top safe area inset is close to zero and the right one carries everything. The fold crosses the display at its physical middle, x = 475.5 pt, which is not the middle of the safe area. items.summary: At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports: China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves: - An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027 - An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028 - A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. items.title: BYD Sold More EVs Last Month Than the US Did All Quarter
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Electrek: The world's leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company's highest monthly total in 2026. BYD's battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. By the end of the year, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. "In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles," adds Electrek. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...
